Omega Squared (Effect Size for ANOVA)

Source: R/omega_squared.R
omega_squared.Rd

Computes the sample omega squared (\(\omega^2\)), Hays' (1994) bias-corrected estimator of the proportion of the population variance of the dependent variable that a fixed effect accounts for, as two estimands: the total \(\omega^2\), a proportion of the total variance, and the partial \(\omega^2\), a proportion of the variance due to the effect and error alone. With estimand = "all", the default, the function reports every estimand its inputs determine; "total" or "partial" reports one. In a one-way design the two are the same number.

Usage

omega_squared(
  object = NULL,
  estimand = c("all", "total", "partial"),
  SS_effect = NULL,
  SS_error = NULL,
  SS_total = NULL,
  MS_error = NULL,
  F_value = NULL,
  df_effect = NULL,
  df_error = NULL,
  N = NULL
)

Arguments

object

Optional. A fitted model of class aov, lm, or aovlist (a multi-stratum fit such as aov(y ~ A + Error(subject/A), data = d)). The function returns one row per effect, with the stratum named for an aovlist. Give either object or summary statistics, not both.

estimand

Which estimand to report: "all" (the default, every estimand the inputs determine, NA for the others), "total", or "partial". An estimand asked for by name that the inputs do not determine is refused (see Details).

SS_effect

The sum of squares of the effect, or a vector of the sums of squares of several effects of one analysis (named for the effects, which label the rows). Given with df_effect and the error mean square.

SS_error

The error (residual) sum of squares, given with df_error as an alternative to MS_error.

SS_total

The corrected total sum of squares, \(\sum (y - \bar{y})^2\) (see the Details of eta_squared). With the sums of squares, it determines the total \(\omega^2\).

MS_error

The error (residual) mean square. Give either MS_error or SS_error with df_error.

F_value

The observed F statistic of the effect, or a vector of the F statistics of several effects tested against the same error term. With df_effect, df_error, and N, it determines the partial \(\omega^2\) only.

df_effect

The numerator degrees of freedom of the effect (one value for each effect, or one for all). Required with F_value and with the sums of squares.

df_error

The error (residual) degrees of freedom. Required with F_value and with SS_error.

N

The total sample size, the number of observations. With the sums of squares or F_value, it determines the partial \(\omega^2\). For an F from a design with an Error() stratum, give the size of the effect's stratum instead (see Details): the number of subjects for an effect tested between subjects, and for an effect tested within subjects the stratum's total degrees of freedom, which is df_effect + df_error when the effect is the only one tested in its stratum. N must be at least df_effect + df_error.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_anova_es, printed through dmar_tbl) with one row per effect and the columns effect, omega_squared_total and omega_squared_partial (only the one asked for when estimand is "total" or "partial"), stratum (for an aovlist fit), F_value, df_effect, df_error, and N. An effect given through the summary interfaces without names is "overall" (or effect_1, effect_2, and so on, for several), and a quantity the inputs do not give is NA. N is the number of observations (for the summary interfaces, N as given); the partial value of an effect of an aovlist fit is computed with the size of its own stratum (see Details), so that its row's F, degrees of freedom, and that size, given to the F interface, reproduce it. The estimand attribute records the estimand asked for, and the estimand_notes attribute names each estimand column that is NA with the reason, which the line beneath the printed table states. tidy() gives one row per effect and estimand (see dmar_tidiers).

Details

The function takes a fitted model (aov, lm, or an aovlist from aov() with an Error() term), the sums of squares of a published ANOVA table, or an F statistic with its degrees of freedom and N. The confidence interval is computed by ci_omega_squared.

Total and partial. For a fixed effect with sum of squares \(\mathit{SS}_{\text{effect}}\) on \(df_{\text{effect}}\) degrees of freedom, error mean square \(\mathit{MS}_{\text{error}}\), corrected total sum of squares \(\mathit{SS}_{\text{total}}\), and N observations, $$\hat{\omega}^2_{\text{total}} = \frac{\mathit{SS}_{\text{effect}} - df_{\text{effect}} \mathit{MS}_{\text{error}}}{\mathit{SS}_{\text{total}} + \mathit{MS}_{\text{error}}},$$ $$\hat{\omega}^2_{\text{partial}} = \frac{\mathit{SS}_{\text{effect}} - df_{\text{effect}} \mathit{MS}_{\text{error}}}{\mathit{SS}_{\text{effect}} + (N - df_{\text{effect}}) \mathit{MS}_{\text{error}}} = \frac{df_{\text{effect}} (F - 1)}{df_{\text{effect}} (F - 1) + N}$$ (Olejnik & Algina, 2000, p. 266 and Table 10, p. 268; Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley, 2027, Eqs. 3.97, 3.98, and 7.44 to 7.46). The total value estimates the effect's share of the total population variance, all other effects and the error included; the partial value estimates its share of the variance due to the effect and the error alone, the variance that remains when the other effects are held constant. Which answers the question depends on whether the design's other factors would vary where the effect is studied (see the Details of eta_squared). In a one-way design \(N - df_{\text{effect}} = df_{\text{error}} + 1\), so the two denominators agree and the estimands are the same number. Some sources print the total's denominator as \(\mathit{SS}_{\text{total}} - \mathit{MS}_{\text{error}}\) (Kim, 2016, Table 4, which gives .326 for an effect whose total \(\hat{\omega}^2\) is .323); the denominator of Hays' estimator adds the error mean square, as here.

Bias correction and negative estimates. The sample \(\eta^2\) is the proportion of sample variance accounted for and overestimates its population value. \(\hat{\omega}^2\) subtracts \(df_{\text{effect}} \mathit{MS}_{\text{error}}\) from the effect's sum of squares and adds to the denominator, which gives an estimator of the population proportion with much smaller bias (Hays, 1994; Olejnik & Algina, 2000; Kelley, 2007). Its numerator is negative whenever F < 1, and a negative estimate of either estimand is reported as 0, since \(\omega^2 \ge 0\) by definition (Olejnik & Algina, 2000, p. 262; Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley, 2027, Section 3.9.2).

What the inputs determine. A fitted model with one error stratum determines both estimands of every effect. Sums of squares determine the total when SS_total is given and the partial when N is given, with df_effect and the error mean square in either case. An F statistic with its degrees of freedom and N determines the partial value only: the total also depends on the sums of squares of the design's other effects, and the function cannot tell from F whether there are any, so the F interface reports the total as NA even for a one-way design, where it equals the partial value. With estimand = "all" an estimand the inputs do not determine is NA, with the reason in the estimand_notes attribute and beneath the printed table; asked for by name, it is refused with an error of class dmar_estimand_undetermined (see dmar_metadata). Sums of squares and F are two ways of giving the same effect, and a call that gives both, or a fitted model with summary statistics, or both MS_error and SS_error, is refused.

Designs. The total \(\omega^2\) is defined for fixed effects in designs whose factors are all between subjects, with one error term (Olejnik & Algina, 2000, p. 266). For an aovlist fit, which has an error term for each stratum, the total is NA; designs with random factors and designs with factors within subjects have \(\omega^2\) formulas of their own (Olejnik & Algina, 2000, Tables 11 and 12; Olejnik & Algina, 2003), which this function does not compute. An interaction or a covariate of an lm fit is an effect like any other, with its own sum of squares and degrees of freedom. The sums of squares of a fitted model are the sequential (Type I) ones of anova(); see the Details of eta_squared on the corrected total, on Types II and III, and on the coding of factors.

Within-subjects designs. An effect of an aovlist fit is tested in its own error stratum, and its partial estimate is computed with the size of that stratum in place of N, the size with which ci_eta_squared and ci_omega_squared convert the limits of its interval: the stratum's total degrees of freedom for an effect tested within subjects, and the number of subjects for an effect in the between-subjects stratum of a mixed design (see the Details of ci_eta_squared). Since \(df_{\text{effect}} (F - 1)\) estimates the noncentrality parameter \(\lambda\) of the effect's test, \(\hat{\omega}^2_{\text{partial}}\) then estimates \(\lambda/(\lambda + M)\), with M the stratum's size, which is the value the sample partial \(\eta^2\) converges to as subjects are added and the quantity whose interval ci_eta_squared(estimand = "partial") reports for the row. Computed with the number of observations N, the estimate of a within-subjects effect estimates \(\lambda/(\lambda + N)\), a smaller quantity, which the sample partial \(\eta^2\) does not estimate. That estimate is the partial \(\omega^2\) that Olejnik and Algina (2003, p. 443) compute for a repeated measures factor, whose N is the total number of observations, and the F interface given the number of rows as N reproduces it. For the three IQ occasions of pygmalion, F(2, 618) with 930 rows gives .150, below the partial \(\eta^2\) of .212 and its interval [.157, .265]; with the stratum's 2 + 618 = 620, the estimate is .209.

References

Bargmann, R. E. (1970). Interpretation and use of a generalized discriminant function. In R. C. Bose, I. M. Chakravarti, P. C. Mahalanobis, C. R. Rao, & K. J. C. Smith (Eds.), Essays in probability and statistics (pp. 35–60). University of North Carolina Press.

Fleishman, A. I. (1980). Confidence intervals for correlation ratios. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 40(3), 659–670. doi:10.1177/001316448004000309

Hays, W. L. (1994). Statistics (5th ed.). Fort Worth, TX: Harcourt Brace College Publishers.

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Kelley, K., & Preacher, K. J. (2012). On effect size. Psychological Methods, 17, 137–152. doi:10.1037/a0028086

Keppel, G. (1991). Design and analysis: A researcher's handbook (3rd ed.). Prentice Hall.

Kim, H.-Y. (2016). Statistical notes for clinical researchers: Sample size calculation 3. Comparison of several means using one-way ANOVA. Restorative Dentistry & Endodontics, 41(3), 231–234. doi:10.5395/rde.2016.41.3.231

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 3 on \(\omega^2\) and Chapter 7 on total and partial \(\omega^2\) in factorial designs.)

Olejnik, S., & Algina, J. (2000). Measures of effect size for comparative studies: Applications, interpretations, and limitations. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 25(3), 241–286. doi:10.1006/ceps.2000.1040

Olejnik, S., & Algina, J. (2003). Generalized eta and omega squared statistics: Measures of effect size for some common research designs. Psychological Methods, 8(4), 434–447. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.4.434

Steiger, J. H. (2004). Beyond the F test: Effect size confidence intervals and tests of close fit in the analysis of variance and contrast analysis. Psychological Methods, 9(2), 164–182. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.9.2.164

Venables, W. (1975). Calculation of confidence intervals for noncentrality parameters. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 37(3), 406–412. doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1975.tb01554.x

Examples

# 1. The sums of squares of a published two-way table: Kim (2016,
#    Table 3), light by material, 2 by 4 with 10 per cell (N = 80).
omega_squared(SS_effect = c(LIGHT = 34.716, MATERIAL = 1996.998,
                            "LIGHT:MATERIAL" = 1570.389),
              df_effect = c(1, 3, 3), SS_error = 2261.612,
              df_error = 72, SS_total = 5863.715, N = 80)
#>  effect         omega_squared_total omega_squared_partial F_value df_effect
#>  LIGHT          0.001               0.001                 1.105   1        
#>  MATERIAL       0.323               0.431                 21.192  3        
#>  LIGHT:MATERIAL 0.250               0.370                 16.665  3        
#>  df_error N 
#>  72       80
#>  72       80
#>  72       80

# 2. An F statistic determines the partial value only. Bargmann's
#    (1970) example, used in turn by Venables (1975), Fleishman (1980),
#    and Steiger (2004): a one-way ANOVA with five groups of 11 and an
#    observed F of 11.221 on 4 and 50 df. In a one-way design the
#    partial value is the total.
omega_squared(F_value = 11.221, df_effect = 4, df_error = 50, N = 55,
              estimand = "partial")
#>  effect  omega_squared_partial F_value df_effect df_error N 
#>  overall 0.426                 11.221  4         50       55

# 3. One-way ANOVA from a fitted model (depression_bdi: three
#    treatment arms, 10 per arm, N = 30); the two estimands agree.
fit_one <- aov(bdi_post ~ condition, data = depression_bdi)
omega_squared(fit_one)
#>  effect    omega_squared_total omega_squared_partial F_value df_effect df_error
#>  condition 0.119               0.119                 3.035   2         27      
#>  N 
#>  30

# 4. Two-factor ANOVA for the manipulated expectancy treatment and the
#    measured grade classification (pygmalion data, unequal cell
#    sizes, N = 310). The treatment by grade interaction is weak here
#    (F = 1.19), so the additive model is used.
fit_additive <- aov(iq_8 ~ treatment + factor(grade), data = pygmalion)
omega_squared(fit_additive)
#>  effect        omega_squared_total omega_squared_partial F_value df_effect
#>  treatment     0.017               0.017                 6.519   1        
#>  factor(grade) 0.028               0.028                 2.787   5        
#>  df_error N  
#>  303      310
#>  303      310

# 5. The same partial values with their confidence intervals.
ci_omega_squared(fit_additive, estimand = "partial")
#>  effect        omega_squared_partial omega_squared_partial_ci_lower
#>  treatment     0.017                 0.001                         
#>  factor(grade) 0.028                 0.001                         
#>  omega_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N  
#>  0.062                          6.519   1         303      310
#>  0.082                          2.787   5         303      310
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
